The normal CDF and PDF (the slides used ggplot2; base R’s curve does fine):

Reproduce: the Bayes / rare disease calculation

A test has a 5% false positive rate and a 0% false negative rate. If 1% of the population has the disease, what is the probability a positive test means disease?

posterior <- function(prevalence, fpr = 0.05, fnr = 0.00) {
  p_pos <- (1 - fnr) * prevalence + fpr * (1 - prevalence)
  (1 - fnr) * prevalence / p_pos
}
posterior(0.01)     # 1% prevalence
## [1] 0.1680672
posterior(0.0005)   # 0.05% prevalence: "think horses, not zebras"
## [1] 0.009905894

Reproduce: the variance of a sample mean, from the operator rules

In lecture we derived \(Var(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n\) using only linearity and the variance rules. Let’s watch the derivation be true:

n <- 25; sigma2 <- 4
means <- replicate(2000, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma2))))
c(simulated = var(means), predicted = sigma2 / n)
## simulated predicted 
## 0.1624133 0.1600000

Reproduce: a computer draws a random variable through the quantile function

Uniform draws pushed through the normal quantile function are normal draws. Same seed, same numbers:

u <- runif(5)
cbind(qnorm(u), {set.seed(1); qnorm(runif(5))}, {set.seed(1); rnorm(5)})[, 2:3]
##            [,1]       [,2]
## [1,] -0.6264538 -0.6264538
## [2,] -0.3262334  0.1836433
## [3,]  0.1836433 -0.8356286
## [4,]  1.3297993  1.5952808
## [5,] -0.8356286  0.3295078
x <- qnorm(runif(10000))
c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), q975 = quantile(x, 0.975))
##          mean            sd    q975.97.5% 
## -0.0002734991  1.0106664451  1.9823129697

Reproduce: probabilities are expectations of indicators

x <- rnorm(10000)
c(mean_of_indicator = mean(x > 1.96), true_prob = 1 - pnorm(1.96))
## mean_of_indicator         true_prob 
##         0.0224000         0.0249979
d <- rbinom(10000, 1, 0.3); y <- 5 + 2 * d + rnorm(10000)
c(direct = mean(y[d == 1]), via_indicator = mean(y * (d == 1)) / mean(d == 1))
##        direct via_indicator 
##      6.995123      6.995123

Reproduce: uncorrelated is not independent

\(X\) is symmetric, \(Y = X^2\). The correlation is zero and \(Y\) is a deterministic function of \(X\).

x <- rnorm(10000); y <- x^2
cor(x, y)
## [1] -0.01312371
plot(x[1:500], y[1:500], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, xlab = "x", ylab = "y = x^2")
abline(lm(y ~ x), col = "red", lwd = 2)          # the best *linear* predictor is flat

Reproduce: the linear projection is what OLS estimates

Even when the conditional expectation is not linear, OLS recovers \(Cov(X,Y)/Var(X)\):

x <- runif(10000, 0, 2); y <- exp(x) + rnorm(10000, sd = 0.3)   # nonlinear CEF
c(projection = cov(x, y) / var(x), ols = unname(coef(lm(y ~ x))[2]))
## projection        ols 
##   3.001022   3.001022

Reproduce: LLN and CLT histograms

The Bernoulli sample-mean histograms from Lecture 1b:

lln_plot <- function(n, p = 0.4) {
  means <- rbinom(1000, n, p) / n
  hist(means, xlim = c(0, 1), col = "beige", main = paste0("n = ", n),
       xlab = "Sample mean")
  abline(v = p, lwd = 3, col = "red")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (n in c(10, 100, 1000)) lln_plot(n)

clt_plot <- function(n, p = 0.4) {
  z <- (rbinom(1000, n, p) / n - p) * sqrt(n)
  hist(z, xlim = c(-2, 2), col = "beige", freq = FALSE,
       main = paste0("standardized, n = ", n), xlab = "")
  curve(dnorm(x, sd = sqrt(p * (1 - p))), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "red")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (n in c(10, 100, 1000)) clt_plot(n)

In-class problem 1: diversification is a variance rule

Two assets have returns with standard deviation 10% each and correlation \(\rho\). From the operator rules, the equal-weighted portfolio has variance \(\sigma^2(1+\rho)/2\).

(a) Simulate 10,000 pairs of returns with \(\rho = 0.9\) (use MASS::mvrnorm), form the portfolio return, and compare its variance to the formula. (b) Repeat for \(\rho = -0.9\). What happened, and why is this “the entire logic of diversification” in one number?

In-class problem 2: mean independent, or just uncorrelated?

Let \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(\varepsilon = X^2 - 1\) (so \(\E[\varepsilon] = 0\)).

(a) Verify by simulation that \(Cov(X, \varepsilon) = 0\). (b) Compute \(\E[\varepsilon \mid X > 1]\) and \(\E[\varepsilon \mid |X| < 0.5]\) from the simulated data. Is \(\varepsilon\) mean independent of \(X\)? (c) One sentence: if \(\varepsilon\) were the error in a regression of \(Y\) on \(X\), which of the two assumptions from lecture would hold, and why does it matter which?

In-class problem 3: total variance in a customer base

A subscription business has two customer segments. Segment A (30% of customers) spends \(\sim \mathcal{N}(80, 10^2)\) per month; segment B (70%) spends \(\sim \mathcal{N}(40, 20^2)\).

(a) Simulate 10,000 customers. Compute the total variance of spending. (b) Compute the two pieces of the law of total variance — the average within-segment variance and the variance of the segment means — and verify they sum to (a). (c) One sentence: if you could only report one of the two pieces to describe “how different are our customers,” which would you pick and why?
